cultivar: Chinary and hybrid seedling bushes plus UPASI clones
processing: Partly oxidised (roughly 30–70% depending on the maker), either twisted or ball-rolled in the Taiwanese manner, and lightly fired; a small speciality line at a few estates.
harvest_season: Year-round; winter and early-summer pickings are the most aromatic.
appearance_dry: Twisted or semi-rolled leaf in mixed brown and olive.
taste_profile: Fruity and mild: peach, honey and a light floral note with a smooth body and gentle astringency.

brewing.notes: Also works gongfu style with short steeps; expect three or four infusions.

vintage_note: Sold in small lots by estate and season (Glendale, Havukal and Chamraj are regulars), usually priced like a good orthodox black from the same garden; drink within a year or two. Styles vary from maker to maker, so read the oxidation description and buy a sample first.
description:
Nilgiri oolong is a small speciality line from a handful of estates in the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu, where a few makers have borrowed Taiwanese and Chinese methods to turn their year-round leaf into something lighter and fruitier than the region's black teas. It is not a traditional product, but it is a real one, and the better lots are worth seeking out.

The leaf is withered, bruised gently and oxidised partway, anywhere from about 30 to 70 per cent depending on the maker, then either twisted or ball-rolled and lightly fired. Because the Nilgiri climate allows plucking all year, oolongs are made in several seasons; the cool winter and early-summer pickings tend to be the most aromatic.

Expect a golden-amber cup with peach, honey and a light floral note, a smooth body and gentle astringency; heavier-oxidised lots lean towards baked fruit, lighter ones towards fresh flowers. Brew it Western style at about 90 °C for three minutes, or gongfu style with short steeps, and expect three or four good infusions.

It is sold in small lots by estate and season (Glendale, Havukal and Chamraj are regulars) at about the price of a good orthodox black from the same garden, and it should be drunk within a year or two. Styles vary a lot, so read the oxidation description and buy a sample first.

A good one to try if you like Darjeeling oolongs or Taiwanese high-mountain teas and want to see what southern India does with the idea.
